claims.text: Chemical and structural stability of AlCrFeNi high-entropy nanoalloys at 800°C is governed by competition between entropy stabilization and oxidation-driven elemental segregation.
Minor Mo doping reduces local oxidation affinity in AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
Suppressing surface oxidation suppresses phase demixing in AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
The initial AlCrFeNi nanoalloys are nanocrystalline.
The as-synthesized AlCrFeNi nanoalloys have a uniform elemental distribution.
High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing environment promotes surface oxidation of AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
Surface oxidation causes elemental segregation in undoped AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
Mo doping locally alters the chemical potential of AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
Mo acts as an oxidation inhibitor in AlCrFeNi nanoalloys.
Inhibition of oxidation by Mo helps maintain a uniform elemental distribution by suppressing oxidation-driven segregation.
After annealing at 800°C in air, undoped AlCrFeNi nanoalloys will exhibit pronounced surface oxidation.
After annealing at 800°C in air, undoped AlCrFeNi nanoalloys will exhibit elemental segregation.
Optimally Mo-doped samples annealed at 800°C in air will exhibit less oxidation than the undoped baseline.
Optimally Mo-doped samples annealed at 800°C in air will retain a more homogeneous phase than the undoped baseline.
Under high-purity argon at 800°C, both doped and undoped alloys will maintain uniform elemental distributions.
The predicted Mo stabilization effect is significant specifically at 800°C in air.
The protective effect of Mo may diminish at lower temperatures.
Prolonged exposure may accelerate oxidation beyond the inhibitory influence of Mo doping.
Excessively high Mo concentrations may produce secondary phases.
Differences between doped and undoped alloys will be more subtle under argon than under air.
